value.overview: The Dark Pewee (Contopus lugubris) is a distinctive flycatcher of the highlands of Costa Rica and western Panama. It is associated with wet montane forests, especially forest edges, clearings, and nearby semi-open areas with tall trees. Usually seen alone outside the breeding period, it hunts from exposed perches and makes short flights to catch insects. Costa Rica contains most of the species’ range, making the country especially important for its global conservation.
value.classification: The Dark Pewee belongs to the tyrant flycatcher family, Tyrannidae, and the genus Contopus. It is closely related to several other large pewees of the highlands of Central America.
value.identification: This is a relatively large, dark pewee with sooty-gray upperparts and a noticeably crested crown. The wings and tail are blackish, with grayish feather edges and a weak wing bar. The throat is pale gray, while the remaining underparts are paler olive-gray, becoming somewhat yellowish on the lower belly. The sexes look alike. Juveniles are browner above and show warmer, rufous-buff edging on some wing feathers.
value.rangeHabitat: The Dark Pewee is endemic to the Talamancan montane region, occurring in Costa Rica and extreme western Panama. In Costa Rica it is resident in the mountains from the Cordillera de Tilarán southward, including suitable areas of the Central Volcanic and Talamanca ranges. It generally occupies wet montane evergreen forest, forest margins, clearings, and adjacent semi-open habitats with tall trees, mostly from about 1,200 to 2,150 meters elevation.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and western Panama; it is not considered a long-distance migrant. Individuals may move locally between forest, edge, and nearby open habitats, but regular seasonal migration is not documented.
value.breeding: The Dark Pewee builds a broad, thick-walled cup or saucer-shaped nest made mainly of mosses and lichens, with a lining of plant fibers. The nest is placed across a branch, usually several meters above the ground, reportedly about 5–18 meters high. The female builds the nest and lays two eggs. Incubation lasts approximately 15–16 days. Adults may defend the nest forcefully, even against larger birds.
value.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on flying insects and other arthropods. It typically waits on a high, exposed perch and makes short sallies into the air to capture prey, often returning to the same lookout. Forest edges, clearings, and semi-open mountain habitats provide suitable hunting positions and may improve access to aerial insects.
value.behavior: Dark Pewees are generally solitary outside the breeding season. They are conspicuous because they often use prominent perches and give a loud, repeated whip-like call. The song has been described as a repetitive, emphatic series of notes. Birds regularly return to favored perches after feeding flights, and breeding adults can become aggressive when defending a nest.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly documented in readily available sources, but the species is not currently assessed as globally threatened.
